with Statement

　The with statement specifies the object to reference when the left side (object) of the . (dot) operator is omitted.

　The syntax is as follows:

with(expression)
    statement or block

　Inside the "statement or block", when the . (dot) operator is used with its left side omitted, the object referenced by that . (dot) operator will be the object specified in the expression of the with statement.


Example:
    with(obj) .member = 1; // Same as obj.member = 1;

    with(obj)
    {
        .member1 = 1; // Assigns 1 to obj.member1
        .member2 = 2; // Assigns 2 to obj.member2
        .member3++; // Increments obj.member3
        .method(); // Calls obj.method
    }

　This statement is particularly useful for reducing typing when setting a large number of properties on an object or calling consecutive methods.

　For example, a script like this:


    var object = new Foo();
    object.setPos(0, 0);
    object.setSize(100, 100);
    object.name = "Unnamed";
    object.color = 0xffffffff;

　can be written as follows:


    var object = new Foo();
    with(object)
    {
        .setPos(0, 0);
        .setSize(100, 100);
        .name = "Unnamed";
        .color = 0xffffffff;
    }

with Statement and Objects

　The expression specified in a with statement is evaluated only once at the beginning when the with statement executes, and thereafter it only references that evaluated result.

　For example, even if you write:


this.dic = %[];
with(this.dic)
{
    .member = 1; // Assigns 1 to this.dic.member
    this.dic = 0; // Assigns something else to dic
    .member = 2; // Assigns 2 to this.dic.member
}

　the second assignment to .member will still succeed. This is because this.dic is evaluated in its initial state when the with statement starts executing, and that evaluated result is used thereafter. It does not re-evaluate this.dic every time.

　Because evaluation happens only once at the start, in use cases where an object is referenced repeatedly, code to reference the object does not need to be generated every time, which can sometimes improve execution speed.

　You can think of the above example as generating code equivalent to the following:


this.dic = %[];
{
    var anonymous_special_local_variable = this.dic;
    anonymous_special_local_variable.member = 1;
    this.dic = 0;
    anonymous_special_local_variable.member = 2;
}

　In a with statement, the result of evaluating the expression is assigned to an anonymous special local variable that can only be accessed via the . (dot) operator with an omitted left side. Thereafter, the . (dot) operator with an omitted left side will reference that "anonymous special local variable".
　The scope holding the result of the expression evaluation can also be considered the same as the local variable scope of the above "anonymous special local variable" (and the scope affected by the with statement behaves accordingly).

The . Operator Outside a with Statement

　When the left side of the . (dot) operator is omitted outside a with statement, it references the global object.
　For example, writing:

.foo = 1;

　outside a with statement has the same meaning as:

global.foo = 1;
